identification.summary: Tianwu is a name given by Taiwanese vendor TeamT5 to a China-nexus threat actor first spotted in 2020 that uses a proprietary modular trojan, Pangolin8RAT [S3]. TeamT5 describes the tool as supporting at least eight communication protocols, and says the group is named after a mythical multi-headed beast [S3][S4]. The Register, reporting on TeamT5's findings, says Pangolin8RAT first appeared in 2019, is regularly updated, and is viewed as a successor to PlugX and ShadowPad [S4].
identification.firstObserved: TeamT5: first spotted in 2020 [S3]. The Black Hat Asia 2022 deck lists the group as active since late 2020 [S1]. Pangolin8RAT itself first appeared in 2019 per The Register [S4].
identification.notes: This is a TeamT5 cluster name. No Microsoft name or MITRE ATT&CK group was found for it. TeamT5 treats it as a possible APT41 (Winnti/Amoeba) subgroup or collaborator, framed as a question in the talk title [S3]. The Black Hat deck lists the group as an Amoeba subgroup with Pangolin8RAT as its tool [S1]. Do not merge Tianwu facts with APT41 facts.

attribution.confidence: TeamT5 labels the actor China-nexus and presents the APT41 relationship as a hypothesis: the conference session is titled 'APT41's New Subgroup?' [S3]. iThome Taiwan reports the link as 'very likely' based on code, tactics and the shared gambling focus [S5].
attribution.basis: TeamT5 reports several TTP overlaps with APT41 [S3]; shared tooling and victim overlap with APT41 and other groups are shown in a TeamT5 Black Hat Asia 2022 deck [S2]; the targeting of gambling operators coincided with Beijing's announced action against such operators, which TeamT5's Silvia Yeh said could be coincidental [S4]. No government attribution to a named PRC agency was found.

regions: Taiwan, the Philippines and Kazakhstan (per Chinese-language iThome report) [S5]
targeting.notes: TeamT5 observed 2020-2021 use of Pangolin8RAT against gaming and gambling, transportation, telecom and government targets in APAC [S3]. A secondary summary of TeamT5 reporting also lists dissidents [S8]; this is not confirmed against the original. The Black Hat deck on the online entertainment industry shows spear-phishing of employees and customer support staff as an initial-access method in that sector [S2]; the deck excerpt reviewed does not tie that technique to Tianwu specifically.

capabilities.summary: Pangolin8RAT is a modular trojan that can download additional DLL plugins from its C2 and, in early versions, supported eight protocols including TCP, HTTPS, UDP, DNS and ICMP [S3][S8]. TeamT5 named the tool from a 'pangolin' string in the PDB path and 'p8rat' in RTTI data [S8]. TeamT5 believes the malware may be shared or traded among Chinese groups, though Tianwu has been its main user to date [S4]. The Black Hat deck lists Cobalt Strike among the group's traits [S1]. A secondary report of a JSAC 2026 talk says Tianwu-linked samples appeared on VirusTotal in September 2025 with added obfuscation and evasion, and refers to a custom Cobalt Strike Beacon; this was not verified against the slides [S9].

diamond.adversary: China-nexus cluster named Tianwu by TeamT5, possibly an APT41 subgroup or collaborator [S3].
diamond.capability: Pangolin8RAT modular multi-protocol trojan; Cobalt Strike; tooling and victim overlap with APT41 [S1][S3][S8].
diamond.victim: Online gaming and gambling, transportation, telecom and government organizations in APAC [S3][S5].
diamond.socioPolitical: TeamT5 notes the gambling-sector targeting coincided with Beijing's action against online gambling operators, possibly by coincidence [S4].
diamond.technology: Windows endpoints and employee or customer-support mailboxes in online entertainment firms [S2].

gaps: Black Hat PDFs, TeamT5 and CYBERSEC pages could not be opened directly (fetch blocked); content is taken from search-result summaries of those pages and may be incomplete [S1][S2][S3].
The primary TeamT5 Pangolin8RAT report was not retrieved.
Sponsor, tasking and strategic objectives are not stated in any source found.
The APT41 relationship (subgroup, collaborator or tool sharing) is unresolved.

Possible overlap with Avast's Operation Dragon Castling (gambling firms in Taiwan, the Philippines and Hong Kong; Avast thanked TeamT5 for IoCs) is suspected from the common sector and region, but no source found links the two. Avast itself assessed a Chinese-speaking APT with moderate confidence and did not name Tianwu [S6][S7].
The 2025-2026 activity claim comes from a social media summary only [S9].
No Microsoft actor name or MITRE group mapping found.
Date of the CYBERSEC 2022 session could not be pinned down (one search summary says 22 September 2022; Black Hat Asia was May 2022).

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain is the online gaming and gambling sector, regional transport and telecom, and government networks in APAC; customer-support and employee mailboxes are an entry point [S2][S3]. STEP 2: The actor's exact objectives are unknown, and the sector mix suggests a mix of commercial and state-interest collection, with the APT41 overlap raising the possibility of financially motivated activity [S3][S4]. STEP 3: Observed pattern is spear-phishing in the entertainment sector, then Pangolin8RAT or Cobalt Strike with DLL plugin loading [S1][S2][S8]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued APAC targeting of gaming, telecom and government with evolving Pangolin8RAT variants. MDCOA is reuse of the shared modular RAT against regional defense-adjacent or telecom targets supporting US partners. Candidate indicators: Pangolin8RAT strings and multi-protocol C2 (TCP, HTTPS, UDP, DNS, ICMP), DLL plugins fetched from C2, and spear-phishing aimed at support staff [S2][S8]. This is a thin evidence base.
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track TeamT5 and APT41-related reporting; the cluster boundary is unsettled so avoid asserting attribution [S3]. (2) Authorities: partner and telecom victims in APAC may require coordination through partner-nation channels. (3) Mission assurance: harden support-desk mailboxes and monitor multi-protocol egress on regional telecom and transport dependencies [S2][S8]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with allies in Taiwan and the Philippines where bilateral agreements allow.
